newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar takes a dive on "Mr Yen" comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar takes a dive on "Mr Yen" comments.

text.p: The dollar took a steep dive in Tokyo trade on Thursday after a Finance Ministry official dubbed "Mr Yen" because of his influence on foreign exchange markets signalled that Japan is not seeking a weaker yen.

The comments by Eisuke Sakakibara, who earned his nickname for his role in helping curb the strength of the yen last year, sent the dollar tumbling nearly two yen from its New York close on Wednesday.
The greenback fell as low as 112.20 yen before recovering slightly to trade around 112.45 yen by mid-morning in Tokyo. It had ended U.S. trading at 113.97 yen.

Sakakibara, director general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, was quoted in a Japanese newspaper as saying that the dollar's correction from its sharp slide last year, which took the greenback to record lows against the yen, was about to finish.

Dollar-selling accelerated when Sakakibara, in later remarks to Reuters, failed to deny the comments attributed to him, to the surprise of some foreign exchange dealers. Instead, Sakakibara said the ministry was closely watching the foreign exchange markets, where the dollar has sharply strengthened recently.

The currency market took his words as a sign that Japan believes the dollar's strengthening cycle has run its course and Tokyo is not interested in seeing a further dollar advance. Emboldened by the comments, dealers rushed to dump the greenback.

"We cannot comment on specific currency levels. We are closely watching current developments," Sakakibara told Reuters. He also said he believes Japan's economy is stronger than the market thinks, and that the pace of decline in Japan's current account trade surplus is slowing.

He declined to comment on the article in the Nikkei Financial Daily newspaper on Thursday which quoted him as saying that the dollar's rise was about to end and that the Finance Ministry was not trying to push the yen down further.

Finance Minister Wataru Kubo, asked separately by reporters to comment on the Nikkei article, said Japan, along with its Group of Seven (G7) partners, was trying to avoid major fluctuations in the foreign exchange market.

Since hitting a post-war global low of 79.75 yen in April last year, the dollar has steadily climbed to above 110 yen, helped by a commitment from leading central banks to seek an "orderly reversal," as well as steps to encourage Japanese capital to flow overseas.

The recent fall in the yen has also been fuelled by record low interest rates in Japan, which have encouraged investors to put their money in higher yielding dollar assets. The strong yen was hurting Japanese exporters by making their products more expensive overseas.
